definition: Staying firmly loyal or determined over time, without giving up or changing sides.
example: Through three losing seasons, the team's steadfast fans still filled the bleachers every Saturday.
nuance: Steadfast praises loyalty that holds up under pressure, while stubborn suggests refusing to change even when you should.
prompt: A student decides whether to keep helping a classmate who is struggling through a hard semester.
options: Maya stayed a steadfast friend, tutoring Leo every week until his grades recovered.
Maya's steadfast support vanished the first time Leo forgot to thank her for helping him.
Leo was so steadfast that he switched his study plan every single afternoon.
Maya is a steadfast walker who always reaches the library before anyone else.
reasons: Helping week after week through a long, hard stretch shows loyalty that never wavers.
Support that disappears at the first disappointment is the opposite of lasting loyalty.
Constantly changing course describes someone fickle, not someone firm in purpose.
The "fast" in this word means firmly fixed, not quick, so speed is beside the point.

practice.prompt: A lighthouse keeper faces a long winter of storms on a remote island.
options: The steadfast keeper climbed the tower stairs in record time to win a bet.
The keeper remained steadfast, lighting the lamp every night despite the constant gales.
Being steadfast, the keeper abandoned the lighthouse after the first rough storm of December.
The keeper's steadfast opinions changed with every suggestion a visiting sailor offered.
reasons: Quickness has nothing to do with it; the word is about firm loyalty and determination.
Carrying out a duty faithfully through hardship shows unshaken resolve.
Giving up at the first sign of difficulty shows a lack of firm commitment.
Views that shift with each new voice are wavering, not firmly held.
